6hCo4S_1Fhw: In February 2012, pro skier Elyse Saugstad was carving through the slopes of the Cascade Mountains when a crack formed in the snowpack above her. Before she was fully engulfed by a 5,000-ton wall of snow, Elyse heard “AVALANCHE!” just in time to react with a lifesaving maneuver. So, how could she survive this crushing snow surge? Avalanches are the rapid descension of snow, ice, rock, or a combination of these down a slope. They can be destructive natural disasters and personal tragedies: in the United States alone, avalanches kill an average of 27 people annually. These alpine nightmares don’t just awaken out of nowhere; they need three specific conditions. First, the mountain needs to have the right slope, typically between 30 and 45 degrees. This is shallow enough to allow snow to build up on the slope, yet steep enough to provide enough potential energy for movement. Second, they typically need a layer of sturdy snow deposited over a weak or unstable layer, or what’s sometimes called “something over nothing.” Take the Cascade Mountain avalanche, where recent heavy storms deposited a nearly 1-meter-deep slab of fresh snow. Below this sat a thin layer of surface hoar. These are delicate, feathery ice crystals that form when water vapor in the air rapidly freezes on the surface of snow, almost like dew in the wintertime. Finally, avalanches need a trigger, something to collapse the weak layer and put the snow in motion. A trigger can be natural, such as heavy snowfall, strong winds, rainfall, or even other avalanches. Or they can be human-caused, like the surface impact of skiers or snowmobilers. Since fractures can propagate quickly through the snowpack, triggers can originate hundreds of meters away— upstream, downstream, or even adjacent to the avalanche’s path. Once in motion, how quickly an avalanche moves depends on the slope’s steepness, its exposure or vegetation cover, terrain roughness, and the type and amount of snow involved. For example, dry, light, and loosely bonded snow tends to travel fast, forming a powder cloud as it moves. In contrast, wet snow avalanches, caused by water moving through the snowpack, travel more slowly but are much denser and can be particularly destructive. Larger avalanches can travel more than 160 kilometers per hour, breaking trees, destroying buildings, and burying roadways. In 1970, one particularly massive avalanche consisting of 50 to 100 million cubic meters of glacial ice, snow, mud, and rock reached speeds of over 300 kilometers per hour. This avalanche proved to be the deadliest in history, engulfing an entire Peruvian town and killing 18,000 people. Avalanches aren't always this large, but even smaller ones can be dangerous for anyone caught in their path. As snow rushes downhill, it can behave like both a solid and a liquid, making its movement difficult to predict. At the fastest-moving front, surface snow moves faster than the snow beneath, pulling victims deep into the snowpack and scattering them across wide areas, making rescue difficult. Once an avalanche slows, the snow loses its fluid-like properties and compacts, leaving victims immobilized and unable to escape on their own. For these reasons, the best way to survive an avalanche is to avoid one altogether. Thankfully, at most ski resorts, parks, and even highways, avalanche workers mitigate risk by continuously monitoring the weather, stability of the snowpack, and human activity. If a threat is detected, they'll close terrain and may even intentionally trigger a controlled avalanche with explosives or artillery. However, there are regions where avalanche risk is not actively mitigated, known as the backcountry. Here, you are responsible for managing your own risk. Local avalanche centers provide avalanche forecasts, and anyone entering the backcountry should understand them, be properly trained, and carry essential rescue gear. And ultimately, in high-hazard terrain, there's no way to completely eliminate risk. The group at the Cascade Mountains consisted of highly experienced skiers. Yet the area was very exposed, and following a large storm, the avalanche danger forecast was elevated. In the end, three skiers lost their lives. But not Elyse, as she was able to deploy an inflatable airbag. These devices are imperfect and a last line of defense, yet can keep a victim closer to the surface, improving their chance of rescue should disaster strike.
QyRqlTV60zM: Imagine a ship struggling in an endless storm. Its captain, though strong and commanding, is a terrible navigator. Neither he nor his crew have been trained to sail, yet they relentlessly vie for control through bribery, flattery, and even mutiny. In the crow's nest sits a true navigator. But her knowledge of the stars, winds, and seasons is dismissed by the crew below. This dysfunctional vessel is the Ship of State— a thought experiment devised by Plato to illustrate his frustration with democracy. Specifically, the kind of democracy practiced in Athens from the 5th to 4th centuries BCE. Unlike the forms of representative democracy practiced today, where voters elect representatives to enact legislation on their behalf, Athenians used a type of direct democracy. While Athenian jurors and most officials were selected by lottery rather than election, every law was voted on directly by the citizens of Athens. Specifically, free men born to Athenian parents— women, foreigners, and enslaved individuals had no voting power. Plato thought this system was destined for ruin. And despite the many differences between Athens’ government and modern representative democracies, many of his fears still ring true today. One of Plato’s two major concerns with direct democracy was its vulnerability to charismatic public speakers. Since laws were voted on in the Assembly, confident orators could sway public opinion for their own benefit. In fact, this kind of speech was considered so powerful a class of paid tutors called sophists emerged to educate wealthy families in the art of persuasion. As a result, Plato felt democracy rewarded the strongest speakers, not those with true political expertise aimed at public welfare. His second concern was democracy's obsession with freedom. In the “Republic,” he outlined how the “license to do whatever one wants” would lead people to prioritize their own desires over the common good. In the short term, Plato believed this would weaken societal cohesion and erode respect for the rule of law. But in the long term, he worried this ever-increasing chaos would lead to a backlash— a yearning for order that would make people vulnerable to a charismatic leader promising stability at the cost of liberty. In Plato’s opinion, all democratic systems were doomed to eventually elect a silver-tongued tyrant who exploits the very freedoms that made democracy possible. Plato’s early solutions to these problems— including handing power to elite philosopher kings— leave much to be desired. But in his final work, “The Laws,” Plato combined democracy and monarchy into a new system he hoped would be stable and enduring. To explain his idea, Plato docked his unruly Ship of State and created a new model: the city of Magnesia. In this imaginary land, everything is designed to counteract the issues of direct democracy, while empowering citizens to be morally and politically engaged. Instead of leaving citizens vulnerable to smooth talkers, Magnesia weaves persuasion directly into its laws. Each law is paired with a “prelude” that outlines the logic behind the law and connects it to shared societal values. For example, Plato feared that false beliefs about the gods would undermine justice. So in Magnesia, atheism and impiety are illegal. But rather than relying solely on the fear of punishment to prevent these crimes, the laws against them contain philosophical arguments designed to convince citizens to adhere to Magnesia’s official religion. Moral education is everywhere in Magnesia, and it’s designed to instill shared responsibility. This way, citizens can retain the individual freedom they value under democracy, but their personal goals are more likely to align with the common good. Even so, Plato still recommends safeguards against corruption. Many of Magnesia’s most powerful positions are held collectively rather than individually. And strict regulations on buying and selling land prevent wealth from pooling in the pockets of an elite minority. Obviously, Magnesia is far from perfect. Plato’s educational regime is borderline cultish, and its constitution requires extremely time-consuming civic engagement from every citizen. Then again, creating an ideal society probably would take time, attention, and education. Your perfect world might not look like Plato’s, but it will likely require a serious commitment from its citizens to guide their Ship of State to a brighter horizon.
